utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, can we have the appearances, please. Sorry. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Matthew Gillett; our Case Manager, Indah Susanti; and legal interns, Jennifer Sorby-Adams and Adrianne Michael.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. It's Christopher Gosnell for Mr. Hadzic this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. First of all, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please state your first and last name, date of birth and ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mate Brletic, born on the 13th of July, 1940, Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brletic, you are about to make the solemn declaration, by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I have to point out to you that by doing so, you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untrue information to the Tribunal. Can I ask you to make the solemn declaration now. The Court Usher will give you the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brletic.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you testify before this trial in the case of Prosecutor and Dokmanovic in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And for Your Honours, the 65 ter number of the testimony is 4705, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you have the opportunity this week in The Hague to review the audio of your testimony from Dokmanovic in a language that you understand and to provide any corrections?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is one correction that needs to be made to the English transcript from Dokmanovic, and this is at transcript page 1325, where it states that 70 per cent of the population of Ilok were in favour of a surrender of arms to the JNA. We discovered this during proofing and we informed the Defence about it, so I'd propose having the witness verify what he in fact said during the Dokmanovic hearing and then we'll, following that, apply to the Registry concerning the transcripts from Dokmanovic, if that's agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Brletic, is it correct that during your testimony in Dokmanovic, you in fact stated that when the referendum was taken, 70 per cent of the population in Ilok were against a surrender of arms to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: That is correct. That is what I stated and made the correction. 70 per cent of citizens declared against a surrender of arms, declared to be against the surrender of arms to the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. With that correction in mind are you satisfied that your testimony from Dokmanovic is accurate and correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I am satisfied my testimony is accurate and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And if you were asked about the same matters today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: They would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter testimony 4705.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1418. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm now going to ask you some additional questions concerning the matters in your testimony. First, could you tell us the approximate ethnic composition of Ilok prior to the conflict in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of Ilok was 12 per cent of Croats [as interpreted], 14 per cent of Slovaks, and the rest were Croats, 76 per cent -- 74 percent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, in the transcript, it has said that 12 per cent of the population was Croats but also that 74 per cent of the population were Croats. Could you confirm which ethnicity were the 74 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 12 per cent were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 74 per cent were Croats of the overall population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, at transcript page 1313 of your testimony in Dokmanovic, you describe the procedure usually followed by the JNA when it attacked villages in the SBWS. You state that they first issued ultimatums, then they used heavy artillery and then entered the villages. In relation to the shelling with heavy artillery, did they target military objectives?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Since there were no military targets in villages, none could have been targeted. Rather, it was businesses, and churches, and buildings where representatives of local authorities were housed that were targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when they entered the villages, which Serb forces would enter?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: When villages were shelled from a certain distance, the shelling was done by the regular forces of the JNA. When the shelling ended, the regular forces of the Yugoslav army would retreat from the village and move on to other tasks. Subsequently, the reservists of the Yugoslav army and -- and local Serbs would enter these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: You referred to the local Serbs and paramilitaries entering villages at transcript pages 1339 to 1340 from your testimony, and you say that they would commit atrocities in the villages. Could you describe what atrocities they would commit.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: When these forces came, and we referred to them as the paramilitary forces, they would come to the villages with the assistance of local Serbs. They would target specific individuals, abuse them physically and psychologically, which would then lead to the worst of all, i.e., murders that they would commit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Which villages did this occur in that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: It was the villages surrounding Ilok and Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please be asked to repeat the witness -- the villages slowly, since he is reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the villages that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Sotin, Tovarnik, Ilaca, Nijemci, Svinjarevci, Cakovci, Boksic, Miklusevci, Dzeletovci, Jankovci, Lovas, Opatovac, Bapska, Mohovo, Sarengrad, Dzeletovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, I see that you're reading from a document, and I'd ask you to answer the questions without referring to this document for the meanwhile, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can I ask what document is in front of the witness? I didn't know that he had anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what -- what document do you have in front of you? What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a document entitled: Persons killed, gone missing, and -- and those who ended up in camps. So it's a list of persons from these villages who ended up in camps, were killed, or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I'm sure that if -- if there are questions in that regard, that the -- the party questioning you will show you documents that are to be eventually exhibits in -- in this case or that are already exhibits in this case. So I would suggest you to put that document away and wait for the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the JNA would first shell villages and then the paramilitaries or, you've said today, reservists, would enter the villages and commit crimes. Did the JNA take any measures to prevent those crimes or to punish the perpetrators of those crimes?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: No. The JNA did not prevent the perpetrators from committing crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Were the JNA and the paramilitaries acting in co-ordination?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: They most probably were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know who these people that you referred to as paramilitaries, and today you've referred to as reservists, reported to?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: They reported to the JNA, in part; that was a part of the reserve force of the former Yugoslavia. Secondly, the insurgent Serbs reported to the government of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this. There's nothing about this in the proofing note, nothing about this in any of the witness's prior statements. I realise I can address it on cross-examination but now evidence has just been elicited that I -- I can only say I'm surprised that there isn't notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the witness's testimony, he describes the actions of the JNA and then paramilitaries, which he has called reservists, coming into villages. So I -- I submit the natural follow-up question is to find out who these people report to. I'd add there is mention in his testimony of the civilian authorities having an ability to influence the actions of these -- these people involved in various actions. So there is some reference to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, with great respect to that, Mr. President, there isn't. And the Prosecution knows that this is directly incriminating. And that element should have been communicated to us and it hasn't been.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours at transcript page 13 - I believe - 39, in his Dokmanovic testimony, to 1340, the witness mentions the that the civilian authorities could have influenced members of the JNA in their actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, whether the civilian authorities could influence the JNA officers is not the same issue that the witness has just testified to. It's a different issue. It's about control over paramilitaries or even influence. The witness testified that the reference that was just given to you by the Prosecution concerns an alleged level of influence by Mr. Dokmanovic over JNA officers. It's an entirely different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, if I could add one more follow-up. Given that the witness has said that these two forces were acting in co-ordination, we would say that the two issues are linked, and it's a natural follow-up to find out who the reporting chain went to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection -- the objection is sustained. And we would ask you, Mr. Gillett, to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, did you personally see members of the JNA together with paramilitary forces at any time?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I saw them at Backa Palanka when I was going to fetch the observers of the European committee, whom I was supposed to escort to Ilok. There, together with the Yugoslav officers, there were representatives, political leaders from an area of Vukovar and Backa Palanka. Mr. Dokmanovic, Kertes, Ljubo Novakovic, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Turning to the events in Ilok, in your testimony at transcript page 1309 to 1310, you described how the inhabitants of surrounding villages such as Sotin, Ilaca, Nijemci fled to Ilok in September 1991. What were the conditions like in Ilok when all these refugees were in that town?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: When these villages fell, many people headed for Ilok in the hope of finding refuge there, since Ilok was peaceful at the time. It was surrounded by the forces of the Yugoslav army which did not engage in combat. The inhabitants of these villages were received by us and accommodated. We secured food supplies for them and provided accommodation for them, and this situation prevailed until Ilok itself had to flee the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you have sufficient supplies of food and electricity for this increase in the population?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: When these refugees, as we called them, arrived from the nearby locations, problems emerged with food supplies and accommodation. We overcame these problems somehow, but the JNA frequently cut off electricity, which we were receiving from the Republic of Serbia. It was thus in their power to cut off electricity. With these intermittent power cuts, we were unable to use various appliances, and we didn't have a supply of water. This was additional pressure at a time when there were more than 20.000 people in Ilok, and all the various settlements around Ilok amounted to more than 10.000 people; in other words, the population of Ilok doubled at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Moving to after the mass exodus on 17 October 1991, what were the conditions like for the Croats who remained in Ilok after this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: The Croats who remained in Ilok were treated by the former authorities of Krajina as citizens of -- second-rate citizens, in fact, because the area was settled by Serbs from elsewhere in Croatian such as Virovitica, Podravska Slatina, et cetera. It so happened that the majority population in Ilok at the time were Serbs, whereas the Croats were a minority. For a while after the exodus, the JNA remained in Ilok. Yugoslav officers found accommodation in those family houses that were better off, where the husbands or the heads of that family had to flee or were absent through some other reasons, and the women who stayed there were forced to put up with these men who they had to cook for and serve them. Certain men were brought in to the police station that had been set up by the SAO Krajina authorities. They were mentally and physically abused. They were questioned about weapons and asked to surrender weapons that they didn't have. The position was that they had hidden the weapons that we had in our possession while we were still in Ilok. Likewise, men were mobilised at a later stage and forced to do labour at the front line in the area of Nijemci. They were forced to do hard labour. They were also beaten and physically and mentally abused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now play video which is Exhibit P322.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The reporter: We are moving to the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. After the press conference, dear viewers, that was held today in Erdut we asked Goran Hadzic, president of the Serb region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem to answer some questions for viewers of the Belgrade television. "Mr. Hadzic, to what extent is the fierce fighting going on now if we can put it that way, in this theatre of war? What are the prospects of this war? "Goran Hadzic: Fights -- the fighting is intense. The first action, the first part, meaning the liberation of Western Srem, is in its final stages. As I said, the fighting for Vukovar is going on. We can say that our units control nearly 50 per cent of the city. We have secure positions and are advancing house by house. The action of mopping of Ustasha villages was also carried out in the last two days. Following the mopping of Sid-Vinkovci section, a couple of Ustasha villages in this section of the central part of our region were mopped up three days ago, so Bogdanovci and the villages done there. Some villages surrender. In Ilok, specifically, one wing is offering to surrender while the other extreme faction will not let them. I will have talks regarding this issue today so they can surrender their weapons and the perpetrators can be held responsible before the law, and the innocent can stay and live with us. "The reporter: Is the territorial army the defenders of the village, the Yugoslav People's Army, launching a stronger offensive since as you yourself are aware there is talk about a great number of complaints with regard to intense war activities, especially by the JNA? "Goran Hadzic: Well, there are complaints. These are, I could say, relatively justified given the attitude and possibilities. Our goal is not a mass killing of Croats but punishing individuals in their midst. This means we have tried everything through democratic and other peaceful means to prevent this. However, even after the signing of the truce, agreements and negotiations, the Ustasha continue disregarding these signatures. It means I do not trust them at all. There can be no negotiation with them so we will have to have some co-ordinated action between the people and the army." The interpreter skipped a passage because it was too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, in the video Hadzic refers to mopping up Ustasha villages. What does this phrase "mopping up" refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. Is this a question about what Mr. Hadzic meant, or is it a question about what the witness understands that phrase to mean, in his own head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please clarify, Mr. Gillett.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, from your experience, what does the phrase "mopping up" refer to?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: As we were looking at this footage of Mr. Hadzic, we could see that he, as one of the politicians, and one of the almost military commanders who had influence on the actions to clear these villages, he could have done something to prevent crimes. The innocent people cannot be blamed that they are ethnic Croats. When this term "mopping up" is used, it is implied that they were searching for Ustashas. We never had Ustashas in our ranks. We never had any troops that belonged to the Home Guards Corps, the ZNG, or the police. When the Serb forces and the Yugoslav People's Army raided our villages - I'll just mention one place, which is Lovas - after the shelling, the residents fled towards Ilok to find refuge. The army withdrew and then paramilitaries came in and perpetrated a crime, almost genocide. They drove 23 men into a minefield. They all got killed. There are records about this case. This is genocide. This is something terrible, an atrocity. And I believe that Mr. Hadzic, who was at the top of that pyramid, the political and the military pyramid in SAO Krajina, could have prevented that crime. He should not have allowed the commander of the police or the paramilitary formations, Ljubomir Devetak from Lovas who directly commanded these forces, to co-operate with Mr. Stanisic who was chief of the state security of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, if I could just ask you to focus on Ilok, which is mentioned in the clip that we've just seen, Mr. Hadzic refers to Ilok and says that he will have talks regarding the surrender of weapons. What is he referring to in that phrase?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. That is asking for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness was based in Ilok at the time and intricately involved in the events there. Mr. Hadzic refers to negotiations and the surrender of arms in Ilok, so I feel the witness is well placed to comment on what that could relate to within the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, the question was: What he is referring to in that phrase. And it's not good enough to say what he could have been referring to. That's exactly what speculation is. It is asking the witness to speculate about what Mr. Hadzic meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Well, I submit it's not pure speculation when Mr. Hadzic refers to a factual event of surrender of arms which is also something commented on in the witness's testimony, and he is in a place to answer whether this could relate to the same facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed with caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I will repeat my question. When Mr. Hadzic refers to having talks regarding the surrender of weapons, do you know what this could relate to?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Well, he probably meant the definitive talks that the JNA was having with the representatives of the civilian and military authorities in Ilok and the surrounding places about the surrender the weapons. In some places these agreements were observed and arms were surrendered, but regardless of the fact that they were surrendered, the paramilitaries came into those places and committed what they committed, what I described. In Ilok, weapons were not surrendered. Instead, we were conducting talks. Never, in the homeland war, I never saw in my area Goran Hadzic or met him as part of a delegation or saw him having talks with us about the surrender of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'm now going to turn to some additional documents concerning events in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: So if I could ask that we get P321 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if the Prosecution is going to make a request for additional time with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I was looking at the clock, Mr. Gosnell, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Indeed. We -- in our most recent exhibit list, we noted that we'd seek 45 minutes with this witness because there are a number of documents that he could comment on, and also in light of the amount of available time in the schedule, we felt that we could, since the witness is here, get him to comment on some relevant documents. So we would seek to have that extra time to address these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Nothing from your side, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This was originally a 92 bis witness. I understand that technically under the Rules here once a 92 bis witness is called for cross-examination they are converted to 92 ter. Under the old Rules once a 92 bis witness was called for cross-examination, it was only for cross-examination. Now I haven't objected in any way and said that they shouldn't also ask clarifying questions, but I am starting to think that we're converting this into a full-blown 92 ter witness, and they're taking a considerable about of time to elicit a lot of information that wasn't in the 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, could I just offer one additional comment before Your Honours consider the issue. The consistent position taken by the Defence in this case from the very beginning has been that documents should come in through witnesses, not bar table motions. We tried to offer a bar table motion shortly before the beginning of the trial which would have covered some of the most non-controversial - in our view - documents. The position consistently taken is, if a witness can speak to documents, the witness should do it. Now, if counsel is agreeing that the documents we'd like to put to this witness today can actually be admitted, be a bar table motion at the end of the trial, then we'll withdraw these now and we can be finished. The Trial Chamber wants to hear the witness comment on them instead, then I propose we go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, just a small point on that, Mr. President. These documents would not have come in through the witness if the 92 bis motion filed by the Prosecution had been granted. So nothing is being taken away here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gillett, we, and the Defence, of course -- - we were on very short notice about the extra time you asked for. We will allow it exceptionally. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could get document P321 on the screen, please. And page -- page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a meeting of 9 October 1991. And you are listed as present at this meeting. About halfway down the page, we see an F. Leko who says that: "... Hadzic has said regardless of negotiations being conducted, he will level Ilok." First, who was F. Leko?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Leko was, at the time, a member of the town assembly in Ilok. And that's his statement. He said that he heard on radio or television that Goran Hadzic had made such a public statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you recall Mr. Leko making that statement at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I recall that he said he had heard a speech by Mr. Hadzic in which Mr. Hadzic had said that he would level Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we now get document 05057 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, this document states that it's a copy of the agreement of 14 October 1991 concerning the exodus from Ilok. Do the terms in this document match those in the agreement that was signed for the departure of the non-Serb inhabitants of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Article 1 refers to the referendum. What was the attitude of the JNA concerning the results of the referendum in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: When the referendum was carried out, the representatives of the Yugoslav army were of course not happy with the result, because they had expected that the result of the referendum would be negative. In reality, it turned out to be a positive vote in favour of the exodus so that all the residents of Ilok would move to the free territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: And why would the JNA be unhappy with the vote in favour of an exodus?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army did not find it in its interest that the population from Ilok and the places I've mentioned move to the free territory of Croatia. There was widespread propaganda by the politicians of SAO Krajina advocating the destruction of all the population in that area and its replacement with Serb population, so that within near future that area could be annexed to Serbia. Whereas, after the referendum and the exodus, it would not remain a part of SAO Krajina. They did not want the Croatian population to stay in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: But I'll repeat: Why would the JNA be unhappy with that outcome?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: The JNA had a completely free hand, and it had plans and designs how to occupy territory. They asked us to surrender weapons. We did not accept that ultimatum. Instead, we agreed that we wanted to remain living in our area in peace and have a free town and a free population and that the JNA may not come into town territory. If the referendum had not been conducted, there would have had to be a direct conflict between the ZNG and the police of Ilok, on one hand, and the Yugoslav army, on the other hand. We would have been in such a position that after that conflict there could be no talks. There would be no one to talk to because, at that time, the Yugoslav army had 25.000 men deployed around Ilok, over 200 artillery pieces, over 100 tanks, which means that it was preparing to completely destroy Ilok. We have guarantees from militaries -- military sources that they were intending to completely destroy Ilok because, on 4 to 5 square kilometres over 150 shells can be fired within one second. So they were able to raze Ilok completely and the entire population would be killed under shelling and under bombing from the air. And that would have been a genocide of the kind that humanity does not remember. And that is why the people of Ilok were forced to flee, to save their women and children, to prevent such a genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: I'll tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1419. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we get document 02094 on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report written by a Mato Baterovic [phoen]. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: He used to be the custodian of the museum in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The report refers to destruction to a number of religious sites listed and I won't run through them except to note that one of them is listed as Orthodox church, Gavrilo, in Sarengrad. Apart from that, do you know what denomination or religion the other churches were?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: They were Catholic and Serb Orthodox churches. And other business premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Which ones were Catholic churches? If we go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: There was the church of Virgin Mary. There was the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get all these names. Could the witness be asked to repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, could you repeat which churches were Catholic churches.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: The Catholic churches were Our Lady's Church, Saint Ivan Kapistran, Saint Paul's Church, another Catholic church in Ilok, Saint George's Church in Bapska. The Orthodox church in Sarengrad. The new church of Nikola Tavelic in Mohovo. All the crosses in Bapska and Sarengrad and in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know who caused the destruction to these religious sites?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: This destruction was perpetrated by the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender this at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1420. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could I check with the Registrar if I have any minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: May I ask a final question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, in your testimony at transcript page 1328 in Dokmanovic, you mentioned that during the exodus on 17 October 1991, you saw him present on the bridge. Did you see any other Serb officials present during that exodus, and who were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is the witness's answer reflected in the proofing note or in any previous statement? I don't know what the witness is going to say. Maybe it is. I'm just -- I would just like to know from the Prosecutor whether they know what the answer is and whether it's reflected in any previous statement or proofing note.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: The answer is something that is, I think, in the testimony at some points but it's not clear, and that's why I'm asking the witness to clarify this matter at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you: Which other Serb officials, if any, did you see during the exodus at the bridge when you saw Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: When the citizens of Ilok were leaving, tents had been placed by the bridge. There were tables and chairs in the tents where refreshments were offered, including sandwiches, for the representatives of the local government in Backa Palanka and the representatives of the SAO Krajina. Mr. Mihalj Kertes was there, as was Dokmanovic, Ljubo Novakovic, the president of the assembly of the Backa Palanka, and the -- an array of the Yugoslav army officers and police officers. It was also noted that there was a representative of the State Security Service of Serbia there, Mr. Stanisic, and his assistant, Mr. Sarac. That was the elite that was present and witnessing something that we can call the expelling of the population of Ilok in the presence of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: That completes my direct examination for this witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gosnell, cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good morning, Mr. Brletic.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic in these proceedings. I'm going to ask you a few questions. If any of my questions aren't clear or you need clarification, please feel free to ask me and I'll try to do that. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Earlier today you testified -- you were asked a question about the term "mopping up," and the answer that you gave was: "When this term 'mopping up' is used it is implied that they were searching for Ustashas. We never had any troops that belonged to the Home Guards, the ZNG, or the police." Do I understand from that answer that you're saying the mopping up was directed at the ZNG or the police or the Home Guard?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Well, it was normal that that should be directed at mopping up the members of the ZNG and the police that happened to be in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you're saying there were none there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Well, it was normal. In all the locations that I mentioned, there were members of the National Guard Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, your testimony earlier was: "We never had any troops that belonged to the Home Guards, the ZNG, or the police." Whom did you mean when you said "we" when you answered that question?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I think that in these villages and the town of Ilok, there was a unit of the National Guard Corps formed - that's to say, the Croatian army - and there were police stations there, there was the police station of Ilok which had its area that it covered all the way to Tovarnik, and that area over there was covered by others. There was the Croatian police in Lovas, Opatovac, and there were also some members of the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, your answer now makes it hard for me to understand your previous answer because you said "we never had any troops that belonged to the Home Guards, the ZNG, or the police." Now you're saying that, in fact, you did have such troops in the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we didn't have the Ustashas and the Home Guards. Those were terms belonging to the Second World War. At that time, there were units of the Ustashas. But this term continued to be used by the Serb population, and members of the ZNG were referred to as the Ustashas. And you know this full well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, that's very helpful. That actually was my primary question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 02216 on the screen, please, which is Prosecution tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in November 1995?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you recognise that what's on the screen in front of you is the first page of that document?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that your signature there on the page?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in signing that statement, did you mean to signify that the contents of the statement were true and correct, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you gave answers that were as complete as possible; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And may I ask you whether the investigator suggested to you that he was interested in any particular individuals when he was talking to you during this interview?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Well, he was probably asking me to say something about specific individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But did he specifically ask you about Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And am I correct in saying that in this statement, as well as in your testimony before the Dokmanovic Trial Chamber in 1998, you identified Mr. Dokmanovic as the president of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, as far as you were concerned, that was the only role that he had, or only position that he had; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Officially he held the position of the president of the assembly. When he left Vukovar, he endorsed the government of the SAO Krajina. What sort of function he occupied there is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, you made no mention of this -- I don't know -- I have no idea what you mean by "endorsed." It doesn't matter. You don't make any mention of Mr. Dokmanovic having any connection whatsoever to any regional government; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Correct. I didn't know which functions he held later because he was not in Vukovar. I had -- but that I had met him with politicians in Palanka, that is a fact. He told me then, Listen, Brletic, can I enter that Ilok of yours? And I told him, Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, let's just stick to the answers to my questions, please. I understand that you want to tell the story again. But you do understand -- and that's understandable, but you do understand that now your testimony from Dokmanovic is in evidence before the Judges, just so you do understand that. So I'm just trying to ask a few specific follow-ups and one of those follow-ups that I'm interested in is -- additional follow-ups is --

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry Your Honour we have an error in transcript. It is in line 23. Instead the word "end" it should be "enter," "Brletic, can I enter that Ilok," not "end that Ilok."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I heard enter, indeed, in the translation, so it's an error in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you realise that at no time in your statement from 1995 or at any time during your testimony in the Dokmanovic case do you make any reference at all to the regional -- the Serbian regional authorities in Croatia? And by that I mean the RSK, the SAO Krajina, or the SAO SBWS.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is it correct that you never saw Mr. Dokmanovic or anyone else who you would say is connected with any of those structures participating in the negotiations for the surrender of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any of them participating in the negotiations concerning Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how many such meetings did you have? I understand that these meetings occurred -- started occurring in September. How many meetings did you have to discuss the fate of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: When I assumed the duty of the commander of the police station in Ilok, I held talks with officers of the Yugoslav army on a weekly basis and as needed; that's to say, with representatives of the Novi Sad corps, Mr. Pero Grahovac. These talks were held weekly and when needed more often as well. As the situation grew ever-more tense and pressure was exerted by the Yugoslav People's Army, to the effect that they wanted to take over Ilok, to take over the power in Ilok, we took this talks to a higher level. We then attended political talks in Backa Palanka, Karadjordjevo, Nestin, Sid, and Vizic. These talks were held with the delegations of both the military and civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: And the subject matter was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, let me stop you there. Am I correct in saying that the -- the -- the political authorities to whom you -- with whom you -- let me rephrase. The political authorities who participated in these discussions was it primarily Mr. Ljubo Novakovic, the president of the Backa Palanka municipality?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And Mr. Kertes?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Kertes was there but rarely at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Any other political authorities participating in any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: There was the president of the Sid Assembly, the president of the local commune of Nestin, of Vizic. Finally, we attended the negotiations with General Arandjelovic in Sid. The negotiations were always conducted in the Serbian territory. They were never conducted in Ilok because neither the government of Sid or representatives of the army wanted to hold these talks in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: During your testimony in Dokmanovic -- well, first of all, let me just ask you: You've testified earlier today that the Yugoslav army had 25.000 men deployed around Ilok. At what time period would you say that they had reached the threshold of having 25.000 men around Ilok?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: That number was reached when the exodus was being prepared. It was several days before the exodus that there was a build-up of the forces of the Yugoslav army, which were deployed, in part, in the territory of Serbia, Principovac, Nestin, Backa Palanka and in the direction of Plavna [phoen]. That was where the Ruma division was. And here there was the Novi Sad corps, Valjevo Corps, and the tank corps which was under the command of General Arandjelovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] and Territorial Defence units from Serbia as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: There were also the reservists who were part of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And one small geographic detail, isn't Principovac on the Croatian side of the border between Serbia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Principovac was occupied by the Yugoslav forces sometime in September. There were minor clashes there, and they simply occupied that area. Our forces were forced to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, sir, I understand that, but the question was just geographic: Is Principovac on the Croatian side of the border or is it on the Serbian side of the border?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Principovac is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, at 28, 17, there is a question -- your question is not on the record. And I don't know whether it is while your microphone was not on, but I think it is important that it would be there, so could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes. The question was: And did that include Territorial Defence units from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in Dokmanovic, and I quote: "Had we not got out then, had we stayed for another two or three days, there would have been a terrible conflict and the entire population would have been destroyed in that area. That was the wish of the Yugoslav officers of the Yugoslav army and of the paramilitary units that were together with the Yugoslav army." What I'm particularly interested is those last few words. Is it true that the paramilitary units were together with the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: It is true. Who was among the reservists was well known. There had to have been paramilitary formations as well. I wasn't able to see them or to see what it was that the Yugoslav army had at its disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And terms of operations, and, first, let me ask you this: How did you know, for example, about the strength of the JNA forces around Ilok? What were your sources of information about that? If you could briefly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Well, listen. You're a soldier. You probably know the composition of the JNA. You know how it works. There are other sources, too. It wasn't just the Yugoslav army that had its sources when analysing the terrain. We had our own professional cadre. And we were able to obtain information as -- about when the attack was imminent and what sort of assets the Yugoslav army had.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Nothing wrong with that at all, sir. Entirely to be expected. But are you saying, then, that you had spies and infiltrators who could give you this information?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: That's only natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And based on the sources that you had, did you know that, in terms of operations, in terms of operational activity, that the JNA was actually giving instructions and orders to these paramilitary units in their operations?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Naturally, I had information to that effect. I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in your testimony in Dokmanovic, you talked at length - and I'm not going to back over it - but you talked at length about the relationship between the Territorial Defence and the JNA and one of the points that you make there is that in some sense the civilian authorities are providing funds for the Territorial Defence. They may have some responsibility for issuing a mobilisation order. But it's true, isn't it, sir, that in terms of operations, the TO is subject to the orders of the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about the movement of the population from Ilok. And if I could, I'd just like to go back to the period prior to the siege of Ilok, if we can describe it that way. Were Serb civilians in Ilok --

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were Serb civilians in Ilok leaving your town at any time during the summer and fall of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: It is true that some individuals of Serb ethnicity left for Backa Palanka and lived there until we left Ilok. What the reasons for their departure were, well, I thought that it was peaceful in Ilok and that there was no pressure to bear on the Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have Prosecution tab 4. Excuse me, Prosecution tab 5, which is 65 ter 374.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, this appears to be a document from the municipality of the city of Ilok. It's dated the 8th of October, 1991. It's directed to the Army Command, the government of the Republic of Croatia. Can I just ask you, when it says the government of the Republic of Croatia, I take it that means the republican government the Croatia, the Croat government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just note. I think the date is 6 October. It's not the greatest printout.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that to the Republic of Croatia government in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Among others. The only Croatian government was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This document is not addressed to anyone in the -- on the -- in the Serb civilian regional governments, is it?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we go over to page 2. Let me just ask before I go on: Did you have anything to do with the drafting of this document?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know anything about how this document was drafted or who it came from?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: The mayor of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you saw it before it was sent, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we go to page 2, paragraph 7: "We invite all of those citizens of Ilok, Serbs and Croats, who, in our opinion, because of individual psychological reasons temporarily have left this community, to return to their homes which we have kept and preserved better than our own." Do I understand from this that after individuals of Serbian ethnicity who left Ilok you and other town officials were protecting the homes that had been vacated?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was involved in that personally. And as the commander of the police, I spoke to these individuals in Backa Palanka one on one. There were meetings held there, which they always attended, and I always told them, Come back to Ilok, because there had been no revenge, nor quarrel between the Serbs, Croats and Slovaks in Ilok. Any such conflicts were prevented, and nobody was ever persecuted for being a Croat, Serb, or Slovak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do see the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Mr. Witness, we take the first break now. We will come back at 11.00. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Brletic, before the break, we were talking about the homes in Ilok that had been vacated by Serbs. Do you remember that discussion?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you explained to us that, in fact, you never discriminated and that you did everything possible to encourage people to come back. And I understand all that. But you didn't answer the precise question I asked you, which was: Did you make efforts to safe-guard the property of individuals who had left.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: All the property, in the ownership of Serbs, was preserved. Nobody moved into those houses. When they came back, they found everything as they had left it. I personally placed police at every place that I had the slightest suspicion that something might happen, where the owner had left for Backa Palanka or Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How many properties are we talking about that had been vacated?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Around 20 houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you testified that -- in Dokmanovic that Ilok normally had a population of between 6- and 7.000 but that after the attacks on Lovas and other villages, that you had an influx of refugees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I have already said that in the area of Ilok, namely, Ilok municipality, including Bapska, San [phoen], and Mohovo villages, there were 9.600 residents also. In the course of the relevant events, some of the Croatian population moved to Croatia proper. Also, 9- to 10.000 people came and the population increased to around 17- to 18.000 before the exodus.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, in your testimony in Dokmanovic, and, of course, it's easy to perhaps not be exact on these numbers, you said that the population had increased to as many as 20.000 people in Ilok itself. Does that refresh your recollection that that may have been a more accurate number, that it was 20.000?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Look, we did not count people. It could be 18- or 20.000. Because we did not count people. That's why I'm saying "roughly," a rough number. Between 18- and 20.000, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And with three times the normal population in the town, conditions must have been extremely crowded; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: The town was really overcrowded. There were not enough beds. We barely managed to find any accommodation. People slept in basements because there was no adequate housing. I said we had water and electricity shortages and outings even before that, and living conditions were very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, yet, your testimony is that you personally placed police in front of the 20 apartments or houses that had been vacated by Serbs to prevent anyone from going inside, notwithstanding these conditions?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because I thought there was a possibility, in view of the fact that people had arrived from those villages. I could not check what kind of people they were, and, of course, I had to protect a number of houses that stood out. Although those people who went to Backa Palanka, they came back occasionally to visit their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, if you did have someone who you thought was appropriate or responsible, would you have considered allowing them to go into one of those vacate houses?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: No. Because we believed that we would resolve the problem in Ilok in a peaceful way. That's why we protected property from intruders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a little bit about the reasons why people -- and the circumstances surrounding the departure of the population from Ilok. And one of the things that you said in your testimony in Dokmanovic was that you were under increasing pressure because you didn't have access to medical services. And one of the things you said in that respect was, and I quote from page 1310 after you've said that in fact you couldn't get to the Vukovar Hospital after a certain stage, you say: "Our other connection was with Novi Sad Hospital which meant negotiating with the JNA for our wounded to be taken to the Novi Sad Hospital but this would have not been feasible because each of our wounded would have been killed." Do you confirm that it's your view that if your wounded had gone over for treatment in Novi Sad, they would have been executed?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: As for health services in Ilok, the situation was very hard. We had only four GPs --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, your testimony from Dokmanovic is before the Judges in this case. They've -- they have it. They can look at it. I asked you a specific question, and we can make this shorter if you just answer the specific question, if it's possible, please.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: It's possible. I will answer. With that agreement with the Yugoslav army prior to departure, the agreement was that if we had any ill or wounded people, we would transfer them to Novi Sad. However, if fighting occurred between the forces of the Yugoslav army and the forces on the Croatian side, we would have been forced, in case we had many wounded, to take them to Novi Sad; but, under circumstances of conflict, those wounded would not be able to get to Novi Sad, and if they were caught, they would probably not survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, to be clear about your testimony from Dokmanovic, you're not talking about a situation of a soldier attempting to -- or being caught in combat. What you're talking about, and I quote: "Negotiating with the JNA for our wounded to be taken to the Novi Sad Hospital." And then your supposition or opinion which you express in Dokmanovic, in the Dokmanovic testimony, is that you believed that "each of our wounded persons would have been killed." So clearly you're talking about the prospects of your wounded being permitted, based on negotiations, to go to Novi Sad Hospital and receive treatment and your belief is that those people -- those people would be killed if they were to be sent there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, my answer was that it is normal in combat, in warfare. There's no agreement. There is no deal. I was talking about a situation before the fighting. I'm -- I'll give you just one example from the Yugoslav army. They had wounded men in the Vukovar Hospital. They wanted me to turn over those men to them. I went to Vukovar. I took that wounded person and took him to Backa Palanka. That is what I did out of my own good conscience. That's natural co-operation without the conflict. Now, if, in case of a conflict I would succeed in turning over the wounded to the other side, that's very hard to say. It happens very rarely in war that the other side gives its wounded to the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So your belief is that, if I understand you correctly, it would not have been possible to negotiate a transfer of wounded to Serbian hospitals because the JNA would have executed those individuals; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Correct. Because amid a conflict, such as it would have been in Ilok, that would have been impossible to do. Because some Yugoslav officers with whom I co-operated, I had a good relationship with them. That's why we were able to work together in peace. However, immediately prior to the conflict, new officers arrived who were not friendly, and that's why I said that the wounded would have been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did other -- did others amongst those who were fighting on the Croatian side in Ilok share that view; if you know?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I did not check that. I was in a command position of the army and the police, and I have my own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: During your testimony in Dokmanovic, you described the reluctance of the JNA to permit to you leave with the population. And what you said there, and I quote from page 1325 was: "The Yugo army did not agree to this exodus, believing that the forces of Ilok, the joint forces of Ilok, were talking the people into leaving. And at that point in time they asked for some kind of a guarantee from us as to why the people were leaving, and it was proposed by the civilian authorities in town to have a referendum carried out who is in favour of surrender and who is in favour of exodus, a complete exodus, from the town of Ilok." Now I understand that this referendum was held on the 13th of October; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how, briefly, was the referendum carried out?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: The referendum was held. It lasted about 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were there written ballots or was this done orally somehow?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: It was a written ballot. There were leaflets where each citizen circled the word "in favour" or "against" in secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what was the question, or questions?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: The referendum was about the exodus. Who is in favour of moving out, and who is in favour of surrendering weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And as far as you were concerned, what did you understand the consequences of surrender to be?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: The consequences of surrendering weapons. We had agreed to surrendered weapons, and I insisted on that on the same day, when the exodus starts at 8.00 a.m. on the day of departure, that weapons should be surrendered. And that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You see, sir, the difficulty I have is I don't understand how these two are mutually exclusive. Why wouldn't it have been possible for you, the fighters in Ilok, to surrender their weapons and leave and then have the civilian population remain behind? Was that an option?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: No. The civilian population decided to go into exodus. If we surrendered weapons, the Yugoslav army would have entered Ilok by force. That's why we agreed. And we obtained guarantees from the Yugoslav army that, as soon as the exodus starts, we would surrender weapons. And there were European observers who supervised all this. And that was a fair way to conduct this action, both for the Yugoslav army and for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, you seem here to be suggesting that there were two choices: Exodus, or the Yugoslav army entering Ilok by force. Wouldn't they only had to enter Ilok by force if you chose to fight?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Of course they would have come in by force. If we had decided to fight, the other side would have fought back, and they were stronger. Of course they would have defeated us. And what would then have happened after the victory the Yugoslav army, I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What about the option of laying down weapons and the population remaining behind?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: We did not even consider that option.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Because we were aware that it was necessary to save the population, that we must not, on any account, get in a clash with the Yugoslav army. It would have been disastrous, fatal to the population. Nobody would have survived with all that shelling and weaponry. When the shelling stopped and when we start to the talk, it's difficult to agree anything different. There's no saving the population or the soldiers. Retaliation begins. We all know how war is waged. We did not leave Ilok of our own free will. It's our wealth. We had 4 million litres of wine in our cellars, just multiply one bottle by ten kunas, the Croatian currency. It's a huge wealth. The other side wanted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I think you've missed my question, because my question wasn't why not get into a clash with the Yugoslav army. My question was: Why not put down your weapons and allow the forces to enter without a clash with the -- with the civilian population remaining behind.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Well, listen, this was the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Why allow the Yugoslav army to take it? We also had our orders from our government in Zagreb. And if one side doesn't give in, conflict occurs. Until then, we had negotiations with the army to leave Ilok alone, and there would be no problem, until a solution is found at the level of the two states. Why would it be in the interests of the Yugoslav army to enter Ilok by force?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What were your orders from the government in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: What orders we had. The government in Zagreb. We were under complete blockade imposed by the Yugoslav army and certain civilian structures from Serbia. We had --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I am sorry to interrupt again. I understand that you want to put it all in context, but the context is there from your testimony in Dokmanovic, respectfully. So if I could just ask you to try, if possible, to focus on what orders you had from the government in Zagreb. What were they?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I don't think I have to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, were there any orders from Zagreb or not? With regard -- with regard to what should happened -- happen in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at the end of the day, Zagreb left it to us to deal with that part alone. We informed Zagreb to the extent of our ability of all our decisions. And colleagues followed it from the area of Serbia. You could see that our assembly decided to let the people of Ilok leave peacefully and move to the free territory of Croatia. We did as they wished, we executed that plan, and we left Ilok.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brletic. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you encourage civilians to leave with you?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Well, that's why we held that referendum, for civilians to state what they wished to do. Nobody forced anyone. One part of the Croats remained. It was a free expression of will. The majority was in favour. And they went with the exodus. Some did not. Some stayed. And quite a few Croats remained in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to take you now to the day of the exodus, as you've described it, and you testified in Dokmanovic, the Dokmanovic trial: "On the bridge, I did not talk to Mr. Dokmanovic because I was too busy with other affairs." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I remember saying that. When I said I was too busy with the other affairs that were ordered to me by the Yugoslav army, because the Saint Ivan Kapistran Church was being targeted. That Yugoslav officer told me, There is a machine-gun nest in the tower of the church. Go and get it down. I told him there was nothing there, so Captain Petrovic and I personally went to the tower of the church and established there was none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brletic, that was a very simple question: Do you remember having said that. So you remembered, but you don't have to repeat everything you said. We saw that in the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And would it be correct you also didn't have an opportunity to observe his -- not only did you not speak to him. You also didn't have an opportunity to see any of his activities that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't either talk to him or was present with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You don't know to whom he may have spoken during that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you have no idea whether he was there on anyone's behalf or in any capacity; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I did -- I have none.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now I'd like to take you to a passage from your testimony in Dokmanovic. I won't pull it up on screen but you said something very striking about Mr. -- or General Arandjelovic. And you described meeting him in what I believe was the definitive meeting before the surrender of Ilok. Can you just confirm, first of all, when it was that you met Mr. -- General Arandjelovic?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I met with him -- was it the 14th or the 15th? I don't know the exact date. The delegation met. There was the referendum that was carried out, and an agreement was reached as to the day when the exodus would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So your meeting with Mr. -- General Arandjelovic was on the same occasion that the agreement was signed for the evacuation of Ilok; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you testified in Dokmanovic, "Can I tell you...," and this is at page 1338: "Can I tell you at one point in time, General Arandjelovic told me personally, 'If you do not surrender weapons with all the arms from tanks, all the arms you have, I am going to use tanks and howitzers and aircraft and I'm going to level Ilok to the ground." And I said, 'Mr. General, you have one daughter. If she is there, would you shoot then?' He said, 'Yes, I would. I am a general and I carry out orders of the General Staff, yes.'" Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's all true, that occurred?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: That's exactly how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And would you say that that statement is consistent with your observation of the kind of man that General Arandjelovic was; that he was a tough, determined military officer?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Very tough and determined and a person who would always implement his intentions. He would always materialise them. And that was a serious threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And your impression was that -- from this statement that his top priority was that he was going to carry out his orders.

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And he was not going to be obstructed by you or anyone else; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could we be a bit specific by what you mean by "anyone else" for the witness, to clarify whether you mean Croat, Serbs, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you sense that he was the kinds of person who would be lightly turned from his object and from his orders?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Of course I did. The way he said it indicated that he was serious. The conclusion was that those of us who were in Ilok had to leave because in the events of combat, we would not leave there alive. This was a serious conversation. He was a serious person. He said that he was a soldier who obeyed the orders of the General Staff. And every soldier must obey the orders of his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And present at this meeting, as I understand it, in addition to General Arandjelovic was Colonel Grahovac, Captain Petrovic, Major Mucalovic, Major Banic, Colonel Ostojic, and the public prosecutor from Sid, as well as Colonel Milic Jovanovic who was from the counter-intelligence service of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was the president of the Backa Palanka municipality, Ljubo Novakovic, also present at that last meeting?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what was General Arandjelovic's attitude towards the one civilian present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't know if the witness can talk about his attitude. Maybe he could be asked about his behaviour towards the representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Attitude as reflected through actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why you're asking me this now. The position of General Arandjelovic was to sign the agreement and act upon it. Which civilians were there did not matter. The only civilian was from the legal profession. And he, together with Grahovac and the president of the commission charged with the referendum, and I was present in part. We drafted the agreement and signed it before General Arandjelovic. He then reviewed the agreement, agreed with it, and said that it should be signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So he was the one in control of -- or representing the Serb side at this meeting and making the decisions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a general, and all his subordinates were obeying him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You testified today at page 17 of the transcript that you heard Mr. Leko, a certain Mr. Leko, make a statement about what he had heard Mr. Hadzic say. Can I, first of all, ask you: Was Mr. Leko at this meeting that we're describing, this final meeting at which the agreement for the evacuation of Ilok was determined?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So when did Mr. Leko make this statement that you described earlier today?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: He stated that at a meeting of the town council in Ilok, because he was the councilman.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was he Croat?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he say where he had heard Mr. Hadzic make this statement?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: He only said that he had heard it over the radio or television. I'm not sure. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you hadn't heard that statement, is that correct, of Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: No, I hadn't heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you're in no position to say here today whether it was said by Mr. Hadzic or not, are you?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just have a moment to consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, did you know that at some point in time in 1991 there were a large number of Serbs forced out of the areas in or around Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MATE BRLETIC
